text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Wednesday. Prepared for Reuters by the Co-operation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The General prosecutor's office officially announced that Culture Minister Rihard Piks breached anti-corruption laws. At the same time it cleared Economics Minister Guntar Krasts.
- Prime minister Shkele accepted the resignation of Piks. The faction of the Farmers Union/Union of Christian Democrats has started discussing new candidatures to the vacant post.

- Prime Minister Shkele went on TV to speak about the political situation in the country. Shkele was critical of parties and said Latvia faced a threat of moral and political bankruptcy and that a new nomenklatura was forming.

- The head of a Chechen delegation, Ahyad Idigov, said the refusal of the Latvian parliament speaker to receive the delegation was an offence to the Chechen people. He also called illegal the refusal of Estonia to issue entry visas to members of the delegation on the pretext they had no valid passports.

- A hunger strike by former workers of the Riga chinaware plant ended yesterday after the bankrupt factory's administrators agreed to pay social tax for the workers which would allow them to receive unemployment benefits.
- The Cabinet discussed the possibility of increasing the minimum wage from 38 to 42 lats from next year.
- The U.S. Senate on Monday backed a proposal that the United States should support the Baltic states, Romania and Bulgaria on their way to NATO.
- New Defence Minister Talavs Jundzis is planning to reduce the 200-men staff of the ministry and to re-organise the headquarters of the armed forces.

- In its commentary to the premier's TV address, the newspaper predicts that Shkele will not quit the political scene but would offer voters a new party, free of corruption and having only one aim: to proceed with reforms.
- The Riga stock exchange and Dow Jones will start publishing an index for the bourse.
